regions.title: Setting Up
regions.summary: Your keyboard, this app, and proof that the two are talking to each other.

gates.title: First contact
gates.objective: Play what the app asks for and see it register.
gates.preview: Everything here is played, not tapped. Before anything else: play the chord shown and watch the keys light up. If they do not, the setup screen will tell you why.

regions.title: Foundations
regions.summary: Triads in every key, and what inversion actually means.

gates.title: Triads
gates.objective: Build a major or minor triad on any root.
gates.preview: A triad is three notes: the root, a third and a fifth. The third is what makes it major or minor — everything else in this game is built on hearing that one note move.

gates.title: Triad inversions
gates.objective: Put any chord tone in the bass, on purpose.
gates.preview: An inversion is not a different chord. It is the same chord with a different note underneath, and the bass is what a listener hears first.

regions.title: Seventh Harmony
regions.summary: The four-note chords the whole language is written in.

gates.title: Seventh chords
gates.objective: Build the six common seventh and sixth chords on any root.
gates.preview: Add one more third on top of a triad and you have a seventh chord. The third and the seventh together are what name it: they are the two notes a jazz musician will not leave out.

gates.title: Seventh inversions
gates.objective: Place the third, fifth or seventh in the bass of a four-note chord.

gates.title: ii-V-I
gates.objective: Play a ii-V-I in any key without working it out first.
gates.preview: Most of the standard repertoire is this progression, moved around. Learn it in one key and you have learned one key; learn what it is made of and you have learned twelve.

regions.title: Jazz Voicings
regions.summary: The shapes a pianist actually plays, rather than the ones a textbook prints.

gates.title: Shell voicings
gates.objective: Play root, third and seventh — and leave the fifth out.
gates.preview: In this exercise the fifth is left out so that the root and the two guide tones sit clearly in the left hand. That is a choice about this voicing, not a rule about the chord.

gates.title: Guide tones
gates.objective: Play the third and seventh alone, and hear the chord anyway.
gates.preview: Two notes are enough to say which chord this is. Once you can hear that, the root belongs to whoever is playing the bass.

gates.title: Rootless voicings
gates.objective: Play the left-hand A position: third, fifth or thirteenth, seventh and ninth.
gates.preview: The A position puts the third lowest. The same four notes rotated give you the B position — they are the same chord, and they do not sound the same.

regions.title: Extensions
regions.summary: Ninths and the colour above the seventh.

gates.title: Ninths
gates.objective: Add a ninth to a seventh chord without losing the chord underneath it.

regions.title: Sus and Slash
regions.summary: Chords with the third taken away, and chords with something else underneath.

gates.title: Suspended chords
gates.objective: Play a suspended chord without the third creeping back in.
gates.preview: A sus chord is a chord with the third replaced rather than removed. The fourth is doing the third's job, and the moment you add the third back the suspension has resolved and the chord is something else.

gates.title: Slash chords
gates.objective: Put a named note in the bass, whether or not it belongs to the chord.
gates.preview: C/E and C/A are written the same way and are two different ideas: one is an inversion, the other is a C chord with an A underneath it. The engine does not guess which you meant, and neither should you.

regions.title: Quartal and Modal
regions.summary: Voicings built out of fourths, where the chord symbol stops being the point.

gates.title: Stacked fourths
gates.objective: Build a fourth-stack over a minor chord, in any rotation.
gates.preview: Stack fourths instead of thirds and the sound stops belonging to one chord symbol. This is the So What voicing: four notes that are a Dm11 on paper and a colour rather than a chord in the ear.

regions.title: Altered Dominants
regions.summary: The colour tones a dominant can take, and the two notes that never move.

gates.title: One alteration
gates.objective: Alter one colour tone of a dominant and keep the guide tones where they were.
gates.preview: An altered dominant is not a new chord to memorise. It is a dominant with one note moved: the third and the seventh stay exactly where they are, and everything else is available.

gates.title: Combined alterations
gates.objective: Alter a ninth and a fifth at once without losing the chord.
gates.preview: Two alterations at once, one of the ninth and one of the fifth. A ninth cannot be flat and sharp at the same time, so the pairs are fewer than they look.

regions.title: Diminished Systems
regions.summary: One symmetrical chord, three forms, and every dominant b9 hiding inside it.

gates.title: Diminished symmetry
gates.objective: Play a diminished seventh from any of its four notes.
gates.preview: A diminished seventh divides the octave into four equal parts, so it sounds the same from any of its notes. There are only three of them in all twelve keys — learn three chords and you have learned all of them.

gates.title: Diminished and the dominant
gates.objective: Hear a diminished seventh as the top of a dominant b9.
gates.preview: Take a dominant b9 and leave out the root: what is left is a diminished seventh. That single fact is why diminished chords resolve the way they do.

regions.title: Substitutions
regions.summary: Putting a different chord where one was, and the shared tones that let you.

gates.title: Tritone substitution
gates.objective: Replace a dominant with the one a tritone away.
gates.preview: Db7 can stand where G7 stood because the two chords share their third and seventh: the third of one is the seventh of the other. The bass moves by a semitone instead of a fifth, and the resolution still works.

gates.title: Secondary dominants
gates.objective: Put a dominant in front of a chord that is not the tonic.
gates.preview: Any chord can be approached as though it were the tonic. Put its own dominant in front of it and you have borrowed a cadence into the middle of a tune — which is most of what makes a turnaround move.

regions.title: Functional Harmony
regions.summary: What a chord is doing, not just what it is called.

gates.title: Diatonic sevenths
gates.objective: Name and play any diatonic seventh chord by its roman numeral.
gates.preview: Seven chords come out of one scale, and each has a job. The numeral is how a musician talks about that job without naming a key — ii is ii in every key there is.

gates.title: The major cadence
gates.objective: Play a ii-V-I in any key, in time.
gates.preview: The ii-V-I is the sentence this whole language is written in. Once it is under your hands in every key, most of a jazz standard is already familiar.

gates.title: The minor cadence
gates.objective: Play a iiø-V-i, where the V brings its own leading tone.
gates.preview: The minor version is not the major one moved down. The ii is half-diminished and the V borrows a raised third that the key does not supply — which is exactly what makes it sound like it is going somewhere.

regions.title: Ear Training
regions.summary: Hearing it before you can see it.

gates.title: Play back what you hear
gates.objective: Reproduce a chord you have heard but not seen.
gates.preview: No symbol on the screen. You hear it, you play it. This is the one exercise where the answer cannot be worked out — only heard.

gates.title: Name the quality
gates.objective: Tell a major seventh from a dominant from a minor, by ear.
gates.preview: Four sounds, one root. The third and the seventh are what change, and they are what your ear is being trained to notice.

gates.title: What changed
gates.objective: Hear two chords and say which tone moved.
gates.preview: Two chords, one note apart. Hearing which note moved is a different skill from naming a chord, and it is the one that makes altered dominants make sense later.

gates.title: Hear the function
gates.objective: Hear a chord in a key and say what it is doing.
gates.preview: The same chord means different things in different keys. This asks for the job, not the name: is that the one, the four, or the five?

regions.title: Reading
regions.summary: Notation, at the speed it goes past.

gates.title: Single notes
gates.objective: Read and play a line of single notes in time.
gates.preview: Pitch and rhythm are scored separately here, on purpose. Playing the right notes late is a timing problem; playing wrong notes exactly on the beat is not.

gates.title: Intervals
gates.objective: Read two notes at once without spelling them out.
gates.preview: Reading an interval is reading a shape rather than two notes. The gap on the staff is the information; the letters are the slow way round.

gates.title: Triads
gates.objective: Read three-note chords on sight.
gates.preview: Three notes stacked is a shape you already know from Foundations. Now it arrives on a staff, at tempo, and you have one beat to see it.

regions.title: Drop Voicings
regions.summary: The same four notes, opened out.

gates.title: Drop 2
gates.objective: Take the second voice from the top down an octave, and keep the chord.
gates.preview: A drop voicing is a close-position chord with one voice moved down an octave. The notes are the same; the spacing is what changes, and the spacing is the sound.

gates.title: Drop 3
gates.objective: Drop the third voice instead, and hear the gap open under it.
gates.preview: Drop 3 leaves a wider hole beneath the upper structure than drop 2 does. It is the guitarist's voicing, and on a piano it is what a left hand does under a melody.

gates.title: Turnarounds
gates.objective: Play a I-vi-ii-V round the loop without stopping.
gates.preview: Four chords that end where they began. A turnaround is what fills the last two bars of nearly every standard, and it loops, so it is the first thing worth being able to play without thinking.

gates.title: iii-VI-ii-V
gates.objective: Start the turnaround from the third degree instead.
gates.preview: The same four bars, entered a step higher. The VI is a secondary dominant now, not a minor chord, and that one alteration is what pulls the whole thing forward.

gates.title: Secondary dominants in a line
gates.objective: Play a chain where each dominant sets up the next chord.
gates.preview: Every chord borrowed a cadence from the chord that followed it. Played as a chain, it is the sound of a bridge in almost any standard.

gates.title: Descending dominants
gates.objective: Play dominants round the cycle, on guide tones alone.
gates.preview: Dominant after dominant, each a fourth above the last, with nothing in your hands but thirds and sevenths. Two notes per chord, and each pair moves by a semitone.

gates.title: The backdoor
gates.objective: Approach the tonic from a whole step below.
gates.preview: iv7 to bVII7 to I. The other way into a major chord, and the reason Bb7 can lead to Cmaj7 without either of them being in the wrong key.

gates.title: Tritone substitution in place
gates.objective: Swap the dominant for the one a tritone away, mid-progression.
gates.preview: You have played the substitute chord. This is playing it where the original stood, which is the only place it is a substitution rather than a chord.

gates.title: Twelve-bar blues
gates.objective: Play a jazz blues through, in several keys.
gates.preview: Twelve bars, three chords, and a hundred years of variation on top. The jazz version adds the ii-V in bars nine and ten and a diminished chord in bar six.

gates.title: Minor blues
gates.objective: The same twelve bars, in minor.
gates.preview: Minor blues is not the major form moved down. Bar nine goes to the flat sixth as a dominant, and the turnaround is darker for it.

gates.title: Rhythm changes
gates.objective: Play the A section of rhythm changes, at tempo, on rootless voicings.
gates.preview: Sixteen bars that half the bebop repertoire is built on. Two chords per bar, rootless voicings in the left hand, and no time to think about any of it.

regions.title: Voice Leading
regions.summary: Getting from one chord to the next without moving more than you have to.

gates.title: Smooth ii-V-I
gates.objective: Move between rootless voicings with the least motion that works.
gates.preview: There are several right answers, and they are not equally good. The one where your hand barely moves is the one a listener hears as one idea rather than three chords.

gates.title: Round the cycle
gates.objective: Keep the voice leading tight through a chain of dominants.
gates.preview: Every chord a fourth above the last, and every voice moving by a semitone or not at all. Done properly your hand stays in one place for the whole cycle.

regions.title: Integrated Reading
regions.summary: Chart in front of you, hands on the keys, no time to translate.

gates.title: Read and comp
gates.objective: Read a chart and comp it in real time.
gates.preview: Everything at once: the chart on the staff, the symbols above it, and a left hand that has to turn both into sound at the tempo the tune is going. This is what all of the above was for.
